unit_label: Module B unit 7 (courseware unit 16): HRM and Information Technology

facts.statement: In the information age, success depends on the ability to access and analyse data into information and extract knowledge and wisdom from it, and an organisation cannot shy away from information technology. HRM has dual responsibility: as a part of strategic HRM, to bring the transformation in mind-set required across the organisation, since technology challenges some of the traditional beliefs and attitudes; and to apply technology to the HR function itself for day-to-day and policy decisions, for which a comprehensive Human Resource Information System (HRIS) is the answer. Information technology is the merging of communication technology and computer technology. IT may change the concept of work (multiple workstations, mainly at homes), organisations may become flatter and leaner, and knowledge workers quite individualistic. The courseware says IT has not diluted the importance of HR: the pressure on quality has increased. IT implementation and HRM are closely inter-dependent: implementation suffered where HRM was improper, and HRM initiatives could not be implemented effectively without change in technology. Utilisation of technology releases excess staff, increases the need for officer staff and renders certain branches and their employees surplus, which has to be managed by HR strategies including an exit policy. The courseware says that banks in India have mostly applied technology to core banking operations and not to the desired extent to HRM and development.

Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) is an umbrella term for technologies combined with the internet, social media, mobile communication and computers, allowing an organisation to renovate its internal processes, structures and core competencies. Information systems have transformed human resource processes and practices, mainly in how organisations collect, store, use and disseminate information; IT brings improvements such as reduced administrative expenses, increased productivity, better decision-making and customer service. HR uses technology for hiring and selecting an individual for an interview, managing employees, storing their data and analysing it; employers use the internet for applications and recruiting. The HR department has to become a learning set-up with self-introspection, sensitivity to environmental changes and openness to new ideas and systems; its first responsibility is to adopt the IT orientation within the department.

Observations that show the need for IT in HR, as the courseware lists them: basic information about an employee is used by many functionaries within and outside HR, so the same database should be shared instead of collecting data from several sources; the database is becoming broad-based (work experience, training, competencies, skills, performance, expectations as well as salary, allowances, increments and leave), making it voluminous; updating can be done partly by different individuals from different locations; decisions (day-to-day or policy) should be embedded in databases to achieve objectivity and consistency, as IT enhances transparency (for example the database can help choose the right person for the right training); policy review requires analysing whether the existing practices function and whether there are biases or prejudices; and statutory requirements need maintenance of such a database. A computer-based Human Resource Information System is the need of the hour, with security measures to ensure confidentiality, integrity, availability and access control of the data. The goal of automation is to help managers work faster and more efficiently; automating business processes reduces administrative work and lets managers focus on managing the workforce.

HR departments need to shift their focus from managing data and records to advising on how processes can be improved and addressing people issues that impact the business, by using new and experimental information. The courseware quotes Bernard Marr: the average HR team is sitting on a data gold mine (recruitment, career progression, training, absenteeism, productivity, personal development review, competency profile and staff satisfaction data) and, when HR data is used to improve decisions, make employees happier and optimise processes, it adds value. HR databases store personal information on employees and can help with recording training details or managing recruitment; the data stored can include employee details, manager information, holiday and absenteeism data, rotas, clocking on and off times, timesheets and expenses. Secure databases let staff access only the data applicable to their job role. The courseware names the modules of one vendor's system as Personnel Manager, Training Manager, Recruitment Manager (for HR or management staff) and Employee Self Service (letting staff contribute to their own HR administration). Reporting functionality allows reports to be run when needs change (recruitment, retirement, promotion, annual pay reviews). HR people should be knowledgeable about how data is stored, managed, retrieved, merged, analysed and reported, as effective consumers of data.

A Human Resource Information System (HRIS) is a systematic way of storing data and information for each individual employee to aid planning, decision making and the submission of returns and reports to external agencies; it is integrated systems used to gather, store and analyse information on an organisation's human resources, merging HRM as a discipline with information technology. The courseware says the major barrier to HRIS success is lack of management commitment and the major limitation the high cost, but the benefits exceed the limitations. Need: decisions on posting, training, compensation, job rotation, promotion and appraisal need the background of the person in terms of competence and training needs; computer-based data makes decisions objective and, when criteria are known and systems used, perceived as unbiased and fair. Advantages listed: effective and realistic evolving of HR policies, programmes and schemes; timely and accurate decisions on promotion, transfer, nomination, provident fund, retirement, gratuity, leave travel concession and earned leave compensation; supplying data and submitting returns to government and statutory agencies with ease; collecting data and converting it to information and knowledge; generating more accurate and real-time HR reports; increasing competitiveness by re-engineering HR processes; improving employee satisfaction by delivering HR services quicker; and providing a comprehensive picture as a single integrated database, giving structural connectivity across units. By automating and devolving routine tasks to line management, HRIS gives HR professionals time for leadership development and talent management. A typical HRIS includes bio-data (name, gender, address, age, insurance policy, blood group), educational and professional qualifications, organisational history (placements, promotions, training, competencies, appraisal) and salary and allowances. Components shown in the courseware's figure are the employee portal at the centre with benefit management, demographics and compensation, time and attendance, applicant tracking, performance management, workflows and communication, and reporting.

Maintenance of the HRIS database: static data (name, date of birth, date of joining) is entered once in a master file, while data on placement and training is upgraded frequently; not all sections are needed by all, so partial access allows several people simultaneous access to sections, and confidentiality of parts such as appraisal data can be maintained through assignment or restriction of permissions in software. The database allows analysis on variables such as age, gender, geographical region and level (for reviews, for deciding placement or career planning by considering past experience and indicating gaps), and is a decision support system. Tools mentioned: Decision Support System (DSS), Expert Systems, Structured Query Language (SQL), Artificial Intelligence, Data warehouse and Data Mining; the database is kept active so that it itself prompts the decision-maker to use it.

facts.statement: A Human Resource Management System (HRMS) is a combination of systems and processes that connect human resource management and information technology through HR software; it can be used in candidate recruiting, payroll management, leave approval, succession planning, attendance tracking, career progression, performance reviews and maintenance of employee information; automation of repetitive tasks frees HR to focus on culture, retention and other impactful areas. Modules can assist with payroll, recruitment and onboarding, gathering and accessing employee information, attendance and absenteeism, performance evaluation, benefits administration, learning management, employee self-service, employee scheduling, and analytics and informed decision making. The courseware says the term HRMS is sometimes used synonymously with HRIS, but a HRIS is really a type of HRMS: a HRIS tracks numerical data and employee information (reporting, training, recruiting, compensation, benefits administration, data tracking, workflow automation and accounting functions), while an HRMS is more robust, comprising IT and HR and also handling non-quantitative information (onboarding, employee satisfaction, job performance, analytics, profitability). Benefits: employees handle some clerical tasks themselves; built-in security including authentication that restricts access; customisable workflow; automated reminders; break-down of bureaucracy and flattening of organisations; and compliance and workflow automation. Signs that a company could benefit: an overworked HR department; losing business and money on HR data or compliance errors; an office spread over locations with no unifying platform; no way to monitor reasons behind turnover or control unengaged employees; and employees who have no responsibility or opportunity to manage their own performance appraisal. Tips for choosing one: understand the basic features and how they address compliance problems; compare vendors; research what meets your needs; determine which gives the best user experience; and assess the vendor as a whole.

e-HRM is the planning, implementation and application of information technology for both networking and supporting HR activities; the integration of all HR systems and activities using web-based technologies; when HR uses the internet or related technologies to support its activities and processes it becomes e-HRM (Strohmeier, 2007: for networking and supporting at least two individual or collective actors in their shared performing of HR activities). In essence it is the devolution of HR operations to management and employees, typically through an intranet or other web-technology channels. Three levels or tiers: operational e-HRM (administrative functions such as payroll and employee personal data); relational e-HRM (also called social e-HRM: supporting business processes such as training, recruitment and selection, and sharing data with managers and others, making virtual relationships among them); and transformational e-HRM (strategic HR exercises such as knowledge management and strategic re-orientation). Its potential is to develop services to internal and external clients, develop efficiency and cost effectiveness and permit HR to become a strategic partner. The main e-HRM activities are: e-recruitment (online recruiting through the company's website or recruitment websites), e-selection (online selection that complies with procedural requirements, using maximum human capital at reduced cost and time), e-performance management (web-based technology to evaluate performance, with a computer monitoring tool or reviews and feedback through a web portal), e-learning (training through the internet or intranet, irrespective of location) and e-compensation (online gathering, storing, analysing and distribution of compensation data, accessible at any time).

HR research is the tool used to evaluate HR practices and performance; it is research conducted in the field of human resources, offering analysis of current development and management issues with real-life case studies. Research is a systematic and scientific process of collecting information, analysing it and drawing conclusions for decisions; the two kinds are applied and academic research, and applied research is conducted to determine HR performance. Types of applied research: the statistical approach (generating statistical standards from existing records to evaluate activities and programmes, discovering the smallest errors); the comparative approach (directly comparing the organisation with another to find areas of poor performance); the outside authority approach (relying on the expertise of a consultant or published research records as the standards for evaluation); and the compliance approach (using samples from the HRIS to find deviations from laws and company policies). HR research can be undertaken to understand trends in existing systems (recruitment, promotion, training, appraisal) and to feel the pulse of the workforce in terms of motivation, commitment, expectations and frustration; a comparison of the applicant population and the selected one can indicate biases; analysis on education, gender and regional representation can support proactive steps; climate or job satisfaction surveys give data for action. In strategic HRM research is an integral component; regular opinion surveys, benchmarking and climate studies have to be conducted to remain sensitive to the internal environment.

Knowledge management (KM) refers to the process of creating, storing, distributing and pooling knowledge (Wilcox, 1997); it is the process of capturing the tacit knowledge of people in a systematic manner for future use. Knowledge workers must be continually re-skilled. The courseware lists five core components to be assessed: people (ability of individuals to influence others with their knowledge), processes (best practices and governance for identifying, managing and disseminating knowledge), technology (to configure and use tools and automate), structure (organisational structures that encourage cross-discipline awareness) and culture (a knowledge-sharing, knowledge-driven culture). It defines KM as the process of creating, identifying and managing knowledge of an organisation and structuring it for effective and efficient use among employees and teams. The courseware says KM matters in banks because competent employees leave for new private sector and foreign banks, and it cites Nonaka and others (1995) on organisational knowledge creation as the capability of a company as a whole to create new knowledge, disseminate it through the organisation and embody it in products, services and systems; an organisation adopting KM as a strategy has to identify knowledge workers (knowledge creators, handlers, processors).

Eight steps for implementing a knowledge management programme (the courseware's list): establish objectives (identify and document the business problems and drivers, short-term and long-term objectives); prepare for change (KM is a culture change; companies that reward only individual performance promote a "knowledge is power" behaviour that contradicts knowledge sharing); define a high-level process (involving the users and contributors); define technology needs; assess the present status of KM in the organisation (the five core components, the gaps and recommendations); draw an implementation plan (re-confirm senior leadership support and funding); implementation stage (celebrate short-term wins); and monitor and measure the KM programme (baseline measures and a balanced scorecard of performance, quality, compliance and value). Benefits of effective KM listed: lower costs; improved decision-making power; easy to find information; tracking ideas, documents and other data; preventing brain drain; learning from mistakes; faster delivery to clients; stimulation of growth and innovation; standardised processes; and better service to employees and customers.

Technology can be used to cost-effectively align employee training with business needs, and developments in technology have increased the potential leverage of the trainer and opened new options for learning; it allows tailoring of training to suit individual learners, cheap mass production of user-friendly learning material and the flexibility to choose time, place and form; it helps distance learning. IT-based training options include interactive multimedia (audio, interactive video, animation, graphics), electronic publishing, video conferencing, computer simulation and virtual reality. Types: virtual instructor-led training (VILT: an instructor-led training converted for online delivery with live sessions or pre-recorded, in real time); e-learning (a learning system using electronic resources, delivered online on any digital device, mostly on learning management system portals: web-based, mobile, gamified, interactive online learning); augmented reality (AR: digital content superimposed on a real-life environment using the device's camera, for example a 360-degree view of heavy equipment, realistic onboarding and cargo loading); and virtual reality (VR: users immerse themselves in a simulated environment using a headset, giving a safe hands-on experience and able to simulate dangerous and risky environments). The courseware says that in banks e-learning is the commonly used method, reaching many employees with timeliness. Advantages of e-learning: study at convenient time and place with privacy and at own pace; high interaction with immediate feedback; can simulate real life; can be cost effective. Disadvantages: relatively inflexible depending on a pre-produced programme; requires greater self-discipline and commitment; may induce a sense of isolation; does not permit personal reinforcement so the motivational effects are forgone; and can prove costly because hardware and software are required.

HR analytics (also workforce analytics, people analytics or talent analytics) is the collection and application of talent data to improve critical talent and business outcomes; it uses analytics tools for decisions related to employees and their effective utilisation, as an important component of business analytics (which focuses on insights into business performance based on huge data and modern statistical methods). HR metrics (for example turnover rates and sick days) are not the same as HR analytics: with analytics HR can gauge employee engagement and whether workers have the skills to reach company goals, interpret data, recognise trends and take proactive steps. The goal is to give an organisation insights for effectively managing employees so business goals are reached, by identifying what data should be captured and how to use it to model and predict outcomes so that the organisation gets optimal return on investment on its human capital. Business intelligence is querying, reporting, online analytical processing (OLAP) and alerts, which answer what happened, how many, how often and where the problem is; analytics answers why it is happening, what if the trends continue, what will happen next (predict) and what is the best that can happen (optimise). The language R is mentioned for handling unstructured data.

Big data is data sets whose size or type is beyond the ability of traditional relational databases to capture, manage and process with low latency; its characteristics are high volume, high velocity and high variety, and its sources include sensors, devices, video and audio, networks, log files, transactional applications, the web and social media, increasingly driven by artificial intelligence, mobile devices, social media and the Internet of Things. Big data analytics examines large and varied data sets to uncover hidden patterns, unknown correlations, market trends and customer preferences to make more informed decisions. Gartner analyst Doug Laney introduced the 3Vs: volume (the amount of data), variety (the number of types of data) and velocity (the speed of data processing); challenges of big data management result from the expansion of all three properties rather than volume alone. The courseware names Apache Hadoop and Apache Spark as open-source tools. Benefits: faster and better decision making; cost reduction and operational efficiency; and an improved data-driven go-to-market (gauging customer needs and risks and creating new products and services).

payload.title: IT and HRM: a two-way dependence
payload.core_explanation_md:
In the information age, success belongs to those who can **access data, turn it into information, and draw knowledge and wisdom from it**. **Information technology** is the **merging of communication and computer technology**.

HRM carries a **dual responsibility**:

| Responsibility | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Change mind-sets** | As part of strategic HRM, bring about the transformation of beliefs and attitudes that new technology demands across the organisation |
| **Use IT in HR itself** | For day-to-day and policy decisions, through a comprehensive **HRIS** |

The two depend on each other: IT projects have **suffered** where HR handling was poor, and HR initiatives **could not be implemented** effectively without technology change.

Likely effects of technology, as the courseware sees them: work may move away from a single office (multiple workstations, mainly at homes); organisations become **flatter and leaner**; workers become knowledge workers, more individualistic. IT **has not reduced the importance of HR**: quantity of staff needed may fall, but pressure on **quality** rises. It also **releases excess staff** and makes some branches surplus, to be managed through HR strategy including an **exit policy**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware observes that in Indian banks technology has mainly been applied to core banking operations and not yet to the desired extent in HR management and development.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the two responsibilities of HRM in the face of information technology?
self_check.expected_takeaway: To bring about the change in mind-set that technology demands, and to apply IT in the HR function itself, through a human resource information system.

payload.title: Why HR needs IT: the case for a shared database
payload.core_explanation_md:
**ICT** (information and communication technologies) is the umbrella for technologies combined with the internet, social media, mobile communication and computers. Its effect on HR is mainly in **how information is collected, stored, used and disseminated**. Benefits: lower administrative expense, higher productivity, better decisions and customer service.

The courseware's observations on why HR needs a database:

1. Many functionaries inside and outside HR use the **same basic employee information**: a **shared database** avoids duplicate collection.
2. The employee record is **broad-based** (experience, training, competencies, skills, performance, expectations, as well as pay, leave and increments), so it is large.
3. Different people can **update parts** from different locations.
4. Decisions should be **embedded in the data** for objectivity and consistency (for example choosing the right person for a training).
5. **Policy review** needs analysis of whether practices work and whether there is **bias**.
6. **Statutory requirements** call for such a database.

The answer: a computer-based **HRIS**, with security measures for **confidentiality, integrity, availability and access control**. The aim of automation is to help managers work faster and focus on managing the workforce.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The HR department itself has to become a learning set-up, with self-introspection and openness to new systems, to lead the organisation in this change.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the four security properties the courseware says an HRIS must protect.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Confidentiality, integrity, availability and access control.

payload.title: HR data and database management
payload.core_explanation_md:
HR teams sit on a **"data gold mine"** (Bernard Marr, as quoted): recruitment, career progression, training, absenteeism, productivity, development review, competency and satisfaction data. Used well it improves decisions, makes employees happier and optimises processes.

**What an HR database holds:** employee details, manager information, holiday and absenteeism data, rotas, clock-in and clock-out times, timesheets and expenses. **Secure** databases let each user see **only the data that applies to their role**; employee self-service lets staff update their own information and so reduces the HR team's burden.

**Maintaining the database:**

| Matter | Practice |
| --- | --- |
| **Static data** | Entered **once** in a master file (name, date of birth, date of joining) |
| **Dynamic data** | Upgraded often (placement, training) |
| **Partial access** | Several people can work on different sections at once |
| **Confidentiality** | Parts such as appraisal data restricted by permissions in software |
| **Analysis** | By age, gender, region, level; helps placement, career planning and reviews |

Tools mentioned: **DSS, expert systems, SQL, AI, data warehouse and data mining**. The database is kept "active" so it prompts the decision-maker to use it.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: HR people need not be data scientists, but they should understand how data is stored, retrieved, merged, analysed and reported so they can be effective users of data.

self_check.prompt_text: Which kind of employee data is entered once in a master file?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Static data such as name, date of birth and date of joining.

payload.title: HRIS: what it is, why it is needed and what it holds
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **Human Resource Information System (HRIS)** is a systematic way of storing data on each employee to aid **planning, decision making and the submission of returns and reports** to external agencies. It is integrated systems to **gather, store and analyse** information on an organisation's human resources, merging HRM with information technology.

**Why needed:** decisions on **posting, training, compensation, rotation, promotion and appraisal** depend on each person's competence and background. Computer-based data makes such decisions **objective**, and when criteria are known they are perceived as **unbiased and fair**.

**Advantages (courseware):** realistic HR policies and schemes; timely, accurate decisions on promotion, transfer, provident fund, retirement, gratuity, leave travel and leave encashment; easy **returns to statutory agencies**; data converted into **information and knowledge**; more accurate **real-time reports**; re-engineered HR processes; faster HR service to employees; a **single integrated database** that connects units. By automating routine tasks and passing some to line managers, HRIS frees HR for **leadership development and talent management**.

**Typical contents:** bio-data, qualifications, organisational history (placements, promotions, training, competencies, appraisal), salary and allowances. **Components** in the courseware's figure: employee portal at the centre; benefit management; demographics and compensation; time and attendance; applicant tracking; performance management; workflows and communication; reporting.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware names lack of management commitment as the major barrier to HRIS and high cost as the major limitation, but says the benefits are greater.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can an HRIS make HR decisions seem fairer?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because decisions rest on computer-based data and known criteria, so they are objective and perceived as unbiased.

payload.title: HRMS versus HRIS: what each does and when a company needs one
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **Human Resource Management System (HRMS)** combines systems and processes that connect HR and IT through **HR software**. It can handle **recruitment and onboarding, payroll, leave approval, attendance, performance reviews, benefits, learning management, succession planning, employee self-service, scheduling and analytics**. Automating repetitive tasks lets HR focus on **culture and retention**.

| | **HRIS** | **HRMS** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mainly tracks | **Numerical** data and employee information | All of that **plus non-quantitative** information |
| Core tasks | Reporting, training, recruiting, compensation, benefits administration, data tracking, workflow automation, accounting | Also onboarding, employee satisfaction, job performance, analytics, profitability |
| Relation | A **type of** HRMS | The more robust system (IT and HR) |

The courseware notes the terms are often used as synonyms and that rebranding has blurred the difference.

**Benefits:** employees do some clerical tasks themselves; **built-in security**, with authentication limiting access; customisable workflow; automated reminders; less bureaucracy.

**Signs a company needs one:** HR is overworked; money lost on HR data or **compliance errors**; offices spread across locations without a unifying platform; no way to monitor **turnover** or control unengaged staff; employees have no opportunity to manage their own appraisal.

**Choosing one:** understand features and compliance needs; compare vendors; research your needs; check user experience; assess the vendor as a whole.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Systems are not "one size fits all": each organisation differs, so the choice must follow the organisation's own needs.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two signs that a company could benefit from an HRMS.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: an overworked HR department; losses from HR data or compliance errors; offices without a unifying platform; no way to monitor turnover; employees unable to manage their own appraisal.

payload.title: e-HRM: three tiers and five activities
payload.core_explanation_md:
**e-HRM** is the planning, implementation and application of IT to **network and support** HR activities: the integration of all HR systems using **web technologies**. In essence it **devolves HR operations to managers and employees**, typically through an **intranet** or other web channels. Strohmeier (2007): IT for networking and supporting at least two actors in their shared performance of HR activities.

**Three tiers:**

| Tier | Concern | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Operational** | Administrative functions | Payroll, personal data |
| **Relational** (social) | Supporting business processes and relationships | Training, recruitment, selection; sharing data with managers; virtual relationships |
| **Transformational** | Strategic HR | Knowledge management, strategic re-orientation |

**Five main online activities:**

| Activity | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **e-Recruitment** | Hiring through the company website or recruitment websites |
| **e-Selection** | Online selection that follows the procedure at lower cost and time |
| **e-Performance management** | Web-based evaluation: monitoring tools, reviews and feedback through a portal |
| **e-Learning** | Training through the internet or intranet, irrespective of location |
| **e-Compensation** | Online gathering, storing, analysing and distributing compensation data, available at any time |

Result: records of employees in different locations are stored together and candidates can be hired from anywhere.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Because e-HRM devolves tasks to employees and managers, it lets HR departments act as strategic partners with better efficiency and cost effectiveness.

self_check.prompt_text: Which tier of e-HRM covers payroll and personal data?

payload.title: HR research: four approaches and what it studies
payload.core_explanation_md:
**HR research** evaluates HR practices and performance, using a systematic, scientific process of collecting information, analysing it and drawing conclusions for decisions. It can be **academic** (adds to the body of knowledge) or **applied** (used to assess HR performance). **Four applied approaches:**

| Approach | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| **Statistical** | Set statistical standards from existing records; even the smallest errors show |
| **Comparative** | Compare your organisation with another to find areas of poor performance |
| **Outside authority** | Use a consultant's expertise or published research as the standard |
| **Compliance** | Use samples from the HRIS to find **deviations from laws and company policy** |

**What HR research studies:** trends in recruitment, promotion, training and appraisal systems; the **pulse of the workforce** (motivation, commitment, expectations, frustration); biases in selection (compare the applicant population with those selected); profile of new entrants against existing staff; education, gender and regional representation; best practices elsewhere.

**Climate and job satisfaction surveys** give data for action, and in strategic HRM research is **integral**: regular opinion surveys, benchmarking and climate studies keep HR sensitive to the internal environment.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A simple analysis can sometimes throw up a problem and show that a policy needs revising.

self_check.prompt_text: Which applied research approach uses HRIS samples to look for deviations from laws and company policy?

payload.title: Knowledge management: five components, eight steps, benefits
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Knowledge management (KM)** is the process of **creating, identifying, storing, distributing and pooling** an organisation's knowledge and structuring it for effective use; in particular, **capturing the tacit knowledge** of people for future use. Knowledge workers must be continually **re-skilled**. In banks the issue is sharpened by competent employees leaving for other banks. An organisation using KM as strategy must first **identify its knowledge workers** (creators, handlers, processors).

**Five core components to assess:**

| Component | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **People** | Individuals' ability to influence others with their knowledge |
| **Processes** | Best practices and governance for identifying, managing and sharing knowledge |
| **Technology** | Tools and automation that enable KM |
| **Structure** | Organisation that encourages cross-discipline awareness |
| **Culture** | A knowledge-sharing, knowledge-driven culture |

**Eight implementation steps:** 1 establish objectives; 2 prepare for **change** (KM is a culture change: rewarding only individual performance breeds "knowledge is power"); 3 define a high-level process; 4 define technology needs; 5 assess present KM status; 6 draw an implementation plan; 7 implement (celebrate short-term wins); 8 **monitor and measure** (baseline and balanced scorecard).

**Benefits (courseware):** lower costs; improved decision-making; easy to find information; tracking ideas and documents; **preventing brain drain**; **learning from mistakes**; faster delivery to clients; growth and innovation; standardised processes; better service to employees and customers.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: KM is more than technology: tools matter, but without a sharing culture and rewards that support it, knowledge stays with individuals.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the five core components of knowledge management to be assessed.
self_check.expected_takeaway: People, processes, technology, structure and culture.

payload.title: Technology in training: VILT, e-learning, AR and VR
payload.core_explanation_md:
Technology lets training be **tailored to individuals**, mass-produced cheaply, and taken at the learner's **chosen time, place and form**, including **distance learning**. Options include interactive multimedia, video conferencing, computer simulation and virtual reality.

| Type | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **VILT** (virtual instructor-led training) | Instructor-led training converted to online delivery, live or pre-recorded, with real-time interaction |
| **e-Learning** | Learning with electronic resources on any digital device, mostly on **LMS portals**: web-based, mobile, gamified, interactive |
| **AR** (augmented reality) | Digital content superimposed on the real environment through a device camera: 360-degree views of heavy equipment, realistic onboarding |
| **VR** (virtual reality) | Immersive simulated environment through a headset: safe hands-on practice, able to simulate **dangerous or risky** places |

The courseware says **e-learning is the commonly used method in banks**, reaching many employees on time.

| Advantages of e-learning | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- |
| Convenient time and place; privacy | Relatively **inflexible** (pre-produced programme) |
| Own pace | Needs **self-discipline** and commitment |
| Interaction with immediate feedback | May cause a **sense of isolation** |
| Can simulate real life | No **personal reinforcement**, so motivational effects are lost |
| Can be cost-effective | Hardware and software can be **costly** |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Different training programmes need different approaches: soft skills may be delivered through web-based training combined with instructor-led sessions.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: inflexible pre-produced content, need for self-discipline, isolation, lack of personal reinforcement, cost of hardware and software.

payload.title: HR analytics, business intelligence and big data
payload.core_explanation_md:
**HR analytics** (also workforce, people or talent analytics) is the **collection and application of talent data** to improve critical talent and business outcomes. It is part of **business analytics**, which uses huge data and modern statistical methods.

**HR metrics are not HR analytics:** metrics (such as turnover rates and sick days) describe what is; analytics lets HR gauge **engagement and skills**, interpret data, spot trends and act early. The goal: insights for managing people so goals are met, by deciding **what data to capture** and **modelling and predicting** outcomes for the best **return on investment in human capital**.

| Business intelligence (BI) | Analytics |
| --- | --- |
| Querying, reporting, OLAP, alerts | **Why** is it happening? |
| What happened? How many? How often? Where is the problem? | **What if** trends continue? What **will happen**? What is the **best that can happen**? |

**Big data** is data whose size or type is beyond traditional relational databases to capture and process with low latency. Gartner's **Doug Laney** set out the **3Vs**:

| V | Meaning |
